title: The Internal Dynamics of Decisions: From Rats and Primates to AI
content: Whether the dynamics that carry a decision to commitment differ between the recurrent circuits of the brain and the transformer networks of large language models is a question about internal dynamics. For any recurrent network there is a feedforward network with matched behavior, so claims resting on internal dynamics must be tested directly. A dynamics demix separates input-driven change from change generated by a population’s own dynamics. Validated first on synthetic systems and checked against the mean-field variance theory of driven echo-state networks, it was applied to cortical populations in perceptual and value-based decisions and to five feedforward transformer language models constructing multi-step answers. Every neural dataset was autonomous-dominated and the five language models were input-dominated; under inference, orbitofrontal cortex recruited its autonomous component on both read-outs (24 of 31 rats on the variance partition), whereas four of the five models did not. For the two models and the cortical dataset re-examined at a matched input dimension of eight, the direction of that difference held. The models’ regime label, however, depends on the dimension of the input basis, so the difference is reported as one of regime at matched input dimension rather than as categorical. After commitment to a perceptual decision the cortical autonomous dynamics became more persistent, more sharply when aligned to the inferred commitment time than to stimulus onset (a specificity supported rather than established); this recovers a transition already reported for these recordings. In the two language models probed layer by layer the correct answer, when detected, first became top-ranked before the output layer, under the read-out used; across generated tokens, no commitment-locked rise in autonomous persistence was found in any model. In a pre-registered control varying only architecture at matched accuracy, the eigenvalue measure separated recurrent from feedforward networks, most cleanly when no input followed the evidence; that control, not the cortex–model comparison, carries the architectural claim. Pre-specified negative tests in orbitofrontal cortex found no commitment signal of the predicted sign in trial-averaged or scalar read-outs. Conclusions are limited to the systems tested. No claim is made about phenomenal experience or machine sentience.
